summary: Defines ASN.X, an XML representation of ASN.1 specifications that avoids many of the ambiguities of ASN.1 syntax and is easier to parse. It works together with RXER. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A tricky instruction book gets rewritten in a tidy format that computers read without confusion. ASN.X is that tidy rewrite.

questions: how to represent asn.1 in xml
why use xml for asn.1 specifications
what are the advantages of asn.x over asn.1
how does asn.x work with rxer
subtitle: XML representation of ASN.1 specifications without ambiguities

tldr.problem: ASN.1 notation is difficult to parse because it has numerous syntactic ambiguities that can only be resolved after parsing the entire specification. This hinders broader adoption of ASN.1.
tldr.mechanism: ASN.X defines a semantically equivalent XML representation of ASN.1 specifications that completely avoids these ambiguities, making specifications much easier to parse and manage using standard XML tools.
tldr.outcome: ASN.X, together with RXER, provides a schema language for XML documents with alternative compact binary encodings. Defined as Experimental in July 2007, it serves as a bridge between ASN.1 and XML-based systems.

today: RFC 4912 remains an Experimental specification. It defines the complete translation of ASN.1 specifications into XML form as ASN.X, compatible with RXER encoding. While technically mature, adoption has been limited, as ASN.1 is typically used in binary encodings and other schema languages have gained broader acceptance in modern system design.

sections.title: The Problem with ASN.1 Syntax
sections.content:
Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) is a complex notation for specifying data structures and communication protocols. However, ASN.1 has numerous syntactic ambiguities: the same notation can mean different things depending on context. For example, certain value notations are indistinguishable from value set notations, object notations, or constraint notations. Disambiguation requires parsing the entire specification.

This parsing difficulty is a barrier to ASN.1 adoption. Implementing a correct ASN.1 parser requires significant engineering effort. A simpler, unambiguous notation would make ASN.1 tools more accessible and easier to build.
sections.plainLanguage: ASN.1 is like a puzzle where some pieces look the same until you see the whole picture. ASN.X fixes this by making every piece look different.

sections.title: ASN.X as an XML Solution
sections.content:
ASN.X is a semantically equivalent Extensible Markup Language (XML) representation of ASN.1 specifications. An ASN.X module is a well-formed and valid XML document conforming to XML namespaces. Because XML has explicit structure and clear delimiters, ASN.X completely avoids ASN.1's inherent ambiguities.

Every ASN.1 construct—types, values, objects, constraints—maps to a specific XML element or attribute. A standard XML processor becomes the foundation of an ASN.1 toolkit. ASN.X definitions can incorporate type and element definitions from XML Schema documents, RELAX NG documents, or DTDs, enabling integration with XML-based systems.
sections.plainLanguage: ASN.X takes the same information as ASN.1 but writes it as clear XML that any computer can read without guessing.

sections.title: Translation Concepts
sections.content:
ASN.X is defined as a set of rules for translating ASN.1 specifications into an XML representation. Each ASN.1 construct (module, type, value, object) maps to XML elements and attributes following a precise set of translation rules.

The translation preserves semantic equivalence: an ASN.1 module and its ASN.X translation are semantically identical. However, an ASN.X module can also be written directly without a pre-existing ASN.1 module, as long as an equivalent ASN.1 module could theoretically exist.

Key translation concepts include: namespace handling through target namespaces and schema identity URIs, reference expansion of parameterized definitions in-line to avoid ambiguities, and annotation elements that translators may use to hold comments or compiler directives.
sections.plainLanguage: There are rules for turning each ASN.1 idea into XML. Both versions mean exactly the same thing, and XML computers understand it perfectly.

sections.title: Structure of ASN.X Documents
sections.content:
An ASN.X module is an XML document with a root <asnx:module> element in the urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:asnx namespace. The module element carries attributes for the module name, target namespace, tag default mode (explicit, implicit, or automatic), and other metadata.

The module contains <import> elements declaring external modules, followed by elements for type assignments (<namedType>), value assignments (<namedValue>), and object definitions. Tags and constraints are represented as nested XML structures rather than as terse notation.

For example, an ASN.1 type MyType ::= INTEGER (0..100) becomes <namedType name="MyType"> with nested elements for the integer type and its size constraint. The structure makes every aspect explicit.
sections.plainLanguage: ASN.X documents are XML with a special root element. Inside are tags for types, values, and objects, all clearly labeled and nested.

sections.title: Representing Types and Values
sections.content:
ASN.1 has many built-in types (INTEGER, BOOLEAN, SEQUENCE, CHOICE, etc.) and ways to constrain or tag them. ASN.X represents each as XML:

  • Built-in types become elements like <type ref="asnx:INTEGER"/>
  • Named types (records with fields) are <sequence> elements with <element> children
  • Enumerated types use <enumerated> with <enumeration> children
  • Constraints like value ranges or size limits become nested elements (<range>, <size>, etc.)
  • Values are either literal values (literalValue="123") or derived from objects

Type definitions can also be tagged (with <tag> attributes) to distinguish values in protocols. All encoding instructions for RXER are handled in the translation but not explicitly shown in the ASN.X document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of data type gets its own XML element. A list of numbers is a <sequence>, choices are <choice>, and rules about what values are allowed go in nested tags.

sections.title: Objects and Information Objects
sections.content:
ASN.1 supports information objects—a way to organize protocol metadata by grouping related types, values, and field definitions. ASN.X represents these as well:

  • Object classes define the structure of an information object (like a class definition)
  • Objects are instances of a class, containing actual values and types
  • Object sets are collections of objects sharing a class

For example, a protocol might define a class with a <field> for a message type and a <field> for its structure. Individual objects then fill in those fields. In ASN.X, these become nested <namedClass>, <namedObject>, and <namedObjectSet> elements with explicit field definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: Objects are like templates with blanks that you fill in. ASN.X makes these templates clear with explicit field elements.

sections.title: Integration with RXER and Encoding Rules
sections.content:
ASN.X, together with Robust XML Encoding Rules (RXER), forms a complete schema language for XML documents. The content of an ASN.X module conforms to the RXER encoding of an abstract ASN.1 ModuleDefinition value. This means an ASN.X module can be decoded using an RXER decoder and re-encoded using any ASN.1 encoding rule (DER, BER, XER, etc.), enabling alternative compact binary encodings.

Other encoding instructions for protocols like GSER (Generic String Encoding Rules) and EXTENDED-XER are represented in ASN.X with <prefixed> elements holding vendor-specific instruction elements. This allows ASN.X to capture encoding-rule-specific directives while remaining human-readable.

The "X" in ASN.X stands for both XML and RXER, reflecting its dual role as an XML notation and an RXER-compatible encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: ASN.X works hand-in-hand with RXER, an XML encoding method. This means ASN.X documents can be converted to compact binary form for efficient transmission, or to other formats.

sections.title: Canonicalization and Normalization
sections.content:
XML canonicalization techniques (such as Canonical XML) ensure that XML documents can be cryptographically signed in a way that survives re-encoding. However, the XML representation (Infoset) of an ASN.X module may change if it is decoded and re-encoded using RXER, even though the underlying ASN.1 value is unchanged. This breaks canonical signatures.

To avoid this problem, ASN.X modules must be normalized prior to the application of syntax-based canonicalization. The normalization rules—which control whitespace, character references, and representation choices—are defined in the RXER specification. Adherence to these rules ensures that canonical representations remain stable across re-encodings.

This is important for applications that rely on digital signatures or integrity checks of specification documents themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: When you sign an ASN.X document, you need to normalize it first so that re-encoding doesn't change the signature. Normalization is like standardizing the formatting before signing.

sections.title: Practical Use and Integration
sections.content:
ASN.X enables several practical improvements over raw ASN.1:

  • Easier parsing: Standard XML processors and libraries can parse ASN.X without specialized ASN.1 parsers
  • Tool integration: XML editing tools, validation tools, and transformation tools (XSLT) can work directly on specifications
  • Schema flexibility: ASN.X modules can reference type definitions from XML Schema or RELAX NG, allowing mixed specifications
  • Compiler directives: Vendors can embed compiler-specific annotations in <annotation> elements using their own namespaces
  • Namespace management: Target namespaces and schema identity URIs provide clear module identity and disambiguation when multiple modules define the same names

Despite these advantages, ASN.X remains Experimental. Adoption has been limited, and the complexity of ASN.1 itself (with its many optional features and extensions) is reflected in ASN.X, making even the XML representation quite elaborate.
sections.plainLanguage: ASN.X lets you use normal XML tools to work with specifications instead of learning special ASN.1 parser rules. You can use standard editors, validators, and scripts.

sections.title: Status and Context
sections.content:
RFC 4912 is an Experimental specification, published in July 2007 alongside related RFCs on RXER and encoding instructions. The document is comprehensive (165 pages) and technically complete, defining the full translation rules for all ASN.1 constructs.

However, ASN.X has not been widely adopted. ASN.1 continues to be used primarily in binary form (DER, BER), and protocol developers often prefer other schema languages like Protocol Buffers or Apache Avro. The complexity of full ASN.1 semantics, even in XML form, creates a high barrier to entry for new tools.

The RFC remains a stable technical reference for those implementing ASN.1-to-XML converters or working with RXER-based systems. It demonstrates how a domain-specific notation can be faithfully translated to XML while preserving all semantic information.
sections.plainLanguage: ASN.X has been available since 2007, but not many people use it. ASN.1 is still used mostly in binary form. If you need to convert ASN.1 to XML, this RFC explains exactly how.
